text: I waded into the flooded library before dawn. The card catalog floated like a raft, drawers coughing wet index cards. Submerged stacks leaned like kelp. A librarian in a diving mask stamped OVERDUE on my wrist and the ink bled into the water.

The childhood kitchen was smaller than memory, linoleum floor sticky with peach jam. The enamel sink dripped in 4/4 time. I opened the breadbox and found a letter addressed to a child who no longer exists. The oven light was a tiny sun that would not set.

I ran the length of an airport with no gates. Every jetway ended in weather. Departures listed cities that are also verbs. A loudspeaker apologized in a language made entirely of boarding tones. My suitcase unpacked itself into paper birds.

A talking moth landed on the lamp and said I had misfiled a year of my life. Its voice was dry paper. It asked whether I preferred the dust of attics or the dust of lecture halls. When I answered, it laid a silver egg of silence on my collar.

I walked a city that is also a piano. The streets were keys, some sticky with rain, some bright as ivory. Buildings were hammers striking from above. When a bus turned the corner it played a minor ninth that made windows open by themselves.

There was a sea inside a hospital. The saltwater corridor smelled of iodine and kelp. Nurses measured the tide instead of blood pressure. In a ward the beds were anchored like boats and a surgeon asked me to hold my breath until the next wave passed.

Back in the flooded library, the talking moth skimmed the water like a skipped stone. It said the dewey decimals had become a tide table. I tried to shelve a book and it opened into a staircase going down through green light.

Mother's kitchen had migrated into the terminal. I stood in the childhood kitchen inside an airport with no gates, stirring soup that tasted of jet fuel and cinnamon. The enamel sink overflowed onto the concourse. No one called my name for boarding.

The piano-city kept modulating. I crossed a boulevard that was a black key and my shoes clicked in dotted rhythms. A street vendor sold metronomes that counted heartbeats. The city that is also a piano asked me, by vibration only, to transpose my name.

In the hospital the sea rose to the nurses' station. Charts dissolved. A doctor floated past holding an otoscope like a periscope. The sea inside a hospital was warm, almost kind, until the PA system announced a code blue for the moon.

I searched the flooded library for a childhood recipe. Between waterlogged stacks I found the linoleum floor of the childhood kitchen, warped into waves. The enamel sink was a baptismal font. Yeast bloomed in the margins of a drowned catalog.

The talking moth rode the luggage carousel in the ungated terminal. The airport with no gates had become a moth sanctuary. It whispered gate numbers that were actually years. I followed 1997 until the carpet turned to grass.

Ambulances were gondolas. I pushed a gurney through the sea inside a hospital while the talking moth perched on the IV pole and recited vital signs as poetry. Salt crusted the call buttons. The moth told me my pulse was a coastal clock.

Downtown, every intersection was a damper pedal. The city that is also a piano flooded from below: not water, but sustain. Chords lingered until pigeons forgot how to land. I played a crosswalk and a tower answered in fifths.

Security asked for a boarding pass written in gravy. I was late, always late, in the airport with no gates. The jetways had vanished overnight. A child sold earplugs that played the sound of a hometown. I bought two and heard my own footsteps arriving.

The childhood kitchen filled with relatives who were also weather. Aunt Hail set the table. Uncle Humidity fogged the windows. I dried dishes that reappeared wet. On the linoleum floor a chalk outline of a loaf of bread waited for an investigation that never came.

Reference librarians wore life vests. The flooded library had a new policy: whisper or drown. I requested a map of tomorrow and received a tide chart stamped with my student ID. Fish swam the aisle markers. One of them was reading.

A waiting room became a harbor. The sea inside a hospital licked the vending machines. I tried to buy ginger ale and received a bottle of night. Orderlies rowed between cubicle curtains. Someone's monitor beeped in 6/8, a lullaby for drowning.

I tuned a skyscraper with a wrench. In the piano city the elevator was a glissando. The streets were keys too wide for human steps, so I crawled, a grace note. The city that is also a piano applauded by dropping a gentle rain of felt.

The talking moth translated the departure board. Each city name shed its vowels. We stood in an airport with no gates while snow fell indoors. The moth's voice scheduled a delay until I remembered why I packed a photograph of an empty chair.

Soup in the childhood kitchen reflected a concourse. I tasted cumin and kerosene. The enamel sink drained into a runway I could not see. Mother hummed a security announcement. I kept stirring as if stirring could open a gate.

Between submerged stacks I found a grand piano lying on its back like a boat. The flooded library used it as an ark. I climbed the lid and played a scale that parted the water just enough to see the call numbers glowing like coral.

MRI rooms were tide pools. Technicians spoke in surf. The sea inside a hospital had claimed imaging: every scan showed coastlines inside the skull. I was asked to lie still while the magnet counted waves instead of protons.

The talking moth insisted I oil the city's hinges. We walked the keyboard of streets at dusk. A talking moth is a poor urban planner, it admitted, but excellent at dusk. The piano-city dimmed to una corda. Shop signs flickered as accidentals.

Customs was a dining table. In the childhood kitchen, officers inspected my pockets for crumbs of the old country. The linoleum floor showed scuff marks shaped like passports. I was allowed to stay if I washed one more plate that would not come clean.

I missed a flight that had no aircraft. The airport with no gates published a poem instead of a schedule. People clapped politely and sat back down. A janitor swept up unused destinations. I kept my boarding pass as a bookmark for a book I had not written.

Night staff floated lanterns down the saltwater corridor. The sea inside a hospital turned gentle, almost lacustrine. I waded to the gift shop and bought a card that said GET WELL in the handwriting of the tide. The cashier was a buoy.

Microfilm readers projected storms. In the flooded library I searched obituaries for the living. Water climbed the call desk. A drowned catalog listed me under both borrower and overdue weather. I signed anyway, in pencil that wrote in currents.

The talking moth taught a seminar on dust. Graduate students took notes that turned into wings. It said scholarship is a kind of molting. I asked about the flooded library and the moth answered that all archives want to become aquariums eventually.

I practiced scales on fire escapes. The city that is also a piano had a blackout, so only the highest windows sounded. Someone in a distant kitchen — not mine — dropped a lid, a cymbal crash. I waited for the dominant to resolve. It never did.

Breakfast was served on a moving walkway that led nowhere. Childhood kitchen smells followed me through the airport with no gates: toast, dish soap, a match just struck. I carried a frying pan as carry-on. TSA waved me through because the pan was humming.

Surgeons operated by moonlight that came from underwater. The sea inside a hospital made every incision shimmer. I was both patient and witness. When they opened the chart, minnows swam out and arranged themselves into a diagnosis I could almost read.

The talking moth rode my shoulder through mother's kitchen. It whispered recipes that were actually directions home. The childhood kitchen accepted this. Yeast rose in the shape of a moth. We baked it, and the bread spoke a single word: stay.

A terminal without gates hosted a recital. The airport had become the first movement of the piano city. Travelers sat on their luggage and listened to taxiways. I clapped when a delayed flight resolved to the tonic of a hometown I no longer claimed.

Reference hours were tidal. I returned a book to the flooded library and it swam away. The sea inside a hospital had leaked into the stacks overnight; IV tubing tangled with the dewey spines. A nurse-librarian shushed the waves. I owed fines in salt.

Linoleum floor, then tarmac, then linoleum again. The childhood kitchen and the airport with no gates were taking shifts as the same room. I packed leftovers for a journey that was only the length of a hallway. The enamel sink reflected departure screens.

I conducted traffic with a baton. Buildings were hammers, yes, but also impatient. The city that is also a piano wanted a cadenza I had not practiced. Rain filled the gutters with overtones. A talking moth kept time on a streetlamp, a dry little click.

Visiting hours coincided with high tide. Relatives arrived in rowboats to the ward. The sea inside a hospital made introductions unnecessary; everyone already floated in the same grammar. I held a bouquet of seaweed and called it hope because the card said so.

I shelved my own childhood in the flooded library, between FOLKLORE and HYDROLOGY. The talking moth proofread the spine labels. Waterlogged photographs curled into boats. I did not check the book out. Some loans are already drowning when you find them.

Gate agents had become choir directors. The ungated airport practiced a hymn about delay. I stood on a moving walkway that was also a keyboard of streets leaking in from the piano-city. My ticket was a chord chart. When I sang the wrong note, the windows opened.

In the childhood kitchen I set a place for the sea. It did not come, but the hospital did: a saltwater corridor opening behind the refrigerator. I poured tea for an absent tide. The linoleum floor buckled into a shoreline. I wiped it as if wiping could ebb.

All six rooms occupied the same night. The flooded library opened onto mother's kitchen, which opened onto an airport with no gates, which opened onto a city that is also a piano. A talking moth led me by the sleeve into the sea inside a hospital and asked, almost kindly, which of these was home. I said the sound they made together, and woke tasting paper and salt.
